points.description: Shows n^k has exactly k digits in base 2n (n^k < (2n)^k, and digits are indexed i=0..k-1; digits at positions ≥k are 0). Also the digit formula: the i-th digit (coefficient of (2n)^i) equals floor(n^k/(2n)^i) mod 2n = floor(n^{k-i}/2^i) mod 2n.

levels.says: Only one of the two: the digit count k, or the digit formula, correctly stated/justified.

points.description: Handles digit i=0: n^k mod 2n = n (since n odd, n^k = n·n^{k-1} with n^{k-1} odd), so digit is n > d for n>d. Any other correct treatment of this case also earns the mark.

For 1≤i≤k-1, writes n^{k-i-1} = 2^i q + r with 0≤r<2^i and r odd (so r≥1) because n is odd (uses oddness essentially), and gets n^{k-i}/2^i = nq + nr/2^i, hence floor = nq + floor(nr/2^i) with floor(nr/2^i) < n. (Equivalent decomposition accepted.)

levels.says: Correct decomposition but does not establish r≥1 / uses oddness incorrectly or omits it.

points.description: Reduces mod 2n: digit = n·(q mod 2) + floor(nr/2^i). If q is odd, digit ≥ n; if q is even, digit = floor(nr/2^i) ≥ floor(n/2^i) ≥ floor(n/2^{k-1}). Concludes all digits > d once n is large.
Chooses an explicit N (e.g. N = 2^{k-1}(d+1), or any N with n/2^{k-1} ≥ d+1 and n>d) and concludes the statement for all odd n>N, covering all digits i=0..k-1.

rubric.notes: Full marks need a complete valid proof; the key idea is using oddness of n to show n^{k-i-1} mod 2^i is nonzero, giving each digit ≥ min(n, floor(n/2^{k-1})). Part marks for correct steps (digit count, digit formula, partial case analysis). A proof that only checks small cases or examples earns little; unjustified claims that digits are large earn nothing for that step.
rubric.answer_key:
Let n be odd, n>N = 2^{k-1}(d+1). Since n^k<(2n)^k, n^k has k digits (positions 0..k-1). Digit i = floor(n^k/(2n)^i) mod 2n = floor(n^{k-i}/2^i) mod 2n.
i=0: n^k mod 2n = n (n^{k-1} odd, so n^k = n·odd ≡ n mod 2n). n>d.
1≤i≤k-1: write n^{k-i-1} = 2^i q + r, 0≤r<2^i; r is odd since n is odd, so r≥1. Then n^{k-i}/2^i = nq + nr/2^i, with 0<nr/2^i<n. So floor = nq + floor(nr/2^i), and floor(nr/2^i)<n. Mod 2n the digit is n(q mod 2) + floor(nr/2^i). If q is odd, digit ≥ n > d. If q is even, digit = floor(nr/2^i) ≥ floor(n/2^{k-1}) ≥ d+1 > d since n > 2^{k-1}(d+1). (For i=k-1: n^0=1, q=0, r=1, digit = floor(n/2^{k-1}).) Hence all digits exceed d. Final: N = 2^{k-1}(d+1) works.
